title: Fix education to make AI work across Europe and Central Asia
gist: The World Bank's Europe and Central Asia Economic Update argues that ECA's AI opportunity, which could partly offset shrinking workforces and two decades of slowing productivity, is bottlenecked by people and skills rather than chips or models. PISA 2025 shows learning quality falling further, with only 29% of ECA students using AI critically versus 45% in the EU, risking a two-speed region.

themes.theme: ECA's AI opportunity and adoption gap

insights.claim: Europe and Central Asia has unusually large potential gains from AI because productivity and business dynamism have slowed for two decades and the working-age population is shrinking in most countries and set to fall sharply by 2060.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: AI-led productivity is framed as a partial offset to demographic drag on ECA growth.
insights.quote: Few developing regions have as much to gain from AI as ECA.
insights.locator: Few developing regions have as much to gain

insights.claim: Fewer than one in ten firms in Europe and Central Asia report using AI in their operations, roughly half the EU average.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Low baseline adoption implies a long runway but also slow near-term AI monetization in the region.
insights.quote: Fewer than one in ten firms report using AI in their operations, roughly half the average in the EU.
insights.locator: At present, AI's potential in ECA

insights.claim: Firms in Europe and Central Asia cite people and skills as the top barrier to AI adoption, and the World Bank argues catching up depends less on chips or advanced models than on human capital.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Suggests compute supply is not the binding constraint for AI diffusion in middle-income markets; skills providers and training matter more.
insights.locator: At present, AI's potential in ECA

insights.claim: Most ECA firms use AI in shallow ways that rarely produce real productivity gains; exceptions such as banks screening loan applications, retailers managing stock and energy producers optimizing inputs invested in skills and data systems and focused managers on results.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: AI productivity payoffs accrue to firms with data infrastructure and results-focused management, a screening criterion for adopters.
insights.locator: What makes AI work

insights.claim: The World Bank contends that the main risk for Europe and Central Asia over the next decade is too little AI adoption, not too much.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Policy bias in the region is likely to tilt toward encouraging rather than restricting AI uptake.
insights.quote: The main risk for ECA over the next decade is too little AI adoption, not too much.

themes.theme: Four ingredients for productive AI use

insights.claim: The World Bank identifies four ingredients for productive AI adoption: workers with foundational skills, vocational education that delivers, managers who can redesign production processes, and workers who keep learning.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: A checklist for assessing which economies can convert AI access into productivity.
insights.locator: Four ingredients stand out

insights.claim: About 45 percent of upper-secondary students in Europe and Central Asia are in vocational programs, more than twice the 22 percent global average and above 70 percent in some countries.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Heavy vocational tracking makes VET quality a key lever for the region's AI-ready workforce.
insights.quote: About 45 percent of upper-secondary students in ECA are enrolled in vocational programs, more than twice the global average of 22 percent
insights.locator: Vocational education that delivers

insights.claim: Research cited by the World Bank suggests about a quarter of productivity gaps between and within countries reflect management practices, and managerial quality is among the strongest predictors of technology adoption.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Management quality is a leading indicator of which firms will extract AI gains.
insights.locator: Managers who can redesign production processes

insights.claim: ECA's average PISA score across math, reading and science fell from about 421 in 2018 to about 406 in 2025, roughly equivalent to losing almost a full year of schooling.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Declining human capital is a structural headwind to long-run productivity growth in the region.
insights.locator: ECA's average score across math

insights.claim: The learning gap between ECA and the EU narrowed from about 3.5 years to 2.5 years, but mainly because EU scores fell by more than ECA scores.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: EU learning outcomes are also falling, a negative signal for European human capital broadly.
insights.locator: The gap with the EU did narrow

insights.claim: In most ECA countries at least half of 15-year-olds score below minimum proficiency versus about one-third in the EU, and in Kosovo, Armenia, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan the share is four in five or more.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Identifies the ECA economies with the weakest future workforce skill base.
insights.locator: The more worrying picture is how many

insights.claim: 4.4 percent of EU students reach the highest PISA proficiency levels, while in ECA only Türkiye comes close and most countries are below 1.5 percent.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: A thin top-talent pool limits ECA's capacity for frontier tech and AI-intensive sectors.
insights.locator: At the top end, 4.4 percent

insights.claim: The share of students who find learning new things interesting fell in every ECA country between 2022 and 2025, and students who skip school score up to two years behind.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Eroding engagement signals the skills decline may persist absent reform.
insights.locator: Student attitudes are also moving

themes.theme: Critical AI use and the two-speed risk

insights.claim: PISA 2025 shows students who check sources and think critically when using AI score about three years of schooling higher than those who accept AI outputs at face value.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: How AI is used, not whether, drives human-capital outcomes, relevant to edtech product design.
insights.locator: AI rewards people who can critically

insights.claim: Only 29 percent of ECA students who use AI take a careful, source-checking approach, compared with 45 percent in the EU.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Quantifies an AI-literacy gap that may widen regional productivity divergence.
insights.quote: Yet only 29 percent of ECA students who use AI take that careful approach, compared with 45 percent in the EU.
insights.locator: AI rewards people who can critically

insights.claim: Using AI simply to summarize texts brings no measurable learning benefit, according to PISA 2025 evidence cited by the World Bank.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Undercuts the value proposition of low-effort AI study tools.
insights.quote: Using AI simply to summarize texts brings no measurable learning benefit.
insights.locator: AI rewards people who can critically

insights.claim: Without education reform, ECA risks becoming a two-speed region where a small educated elite captures most AI gains while the majority falls behind as AI spreads into more work, a problem later spending cannot fully fix.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: AI could widen inequality in ECA, with social and political second-order effects.
insights.locator: The risk is a two-speed region

insights.claim: Today's 15-year-olds are the workers and managers who must make AI work in the 2030s, so weak foundational skills now imply shallow AI use in the region next decade.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Education quality today is a leading indicator for 2030s AI productivity.
insights.locator: Today's 15-year-olds are the workers

insights.claim: Türkiye, Montenegro, Georgia and Uzbekistan are among the six countries with the largest PISA improvements worldwide, showing the decline is reversible.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: These countries are improving their human-capital trajectory relative to regional peers.
insights.locator: The good news is that the decline

insights.claim: Türkiye paired digital infrastructure investment with a curriculum shift from memorization toward real-world problem solving.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: A template for policy-driven skill gains alongside digital investment.
insights.locator: The good news is that the decline

insights.claim: Uzbekistan set a target of reaching the PISA top 30, reformed curriculum and teacher training, banned phones in schools, and expanded early childhood education coverage from 30 to 75 percent.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Uzbekistan's reform momentum supports its medium-term human-capital story.
insights.locator: The good news is that the decline

insights.claim: The World Bank recommends securing early foundational learning, teaching students to question AI, limiting device distraction in schools, cultivating curiosity, and retraining current workers and managers in foundational, digital and managerial skills.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Signals policy demand for early-childhood, teacher-training and upskilling services in ECA.
insights.locator: These priorities emerge for ECA countries

insights.claim: The authors argue compute, data and investment matter, but education is decisive for whether AI amplifies thinking rather than substitutes for it.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Human-capital policy, not infrastructure alone, determines AI returns in emerging Europe and Central Asia.
